nameStory: Creeping Fingerwort gets its name from its delicate, finger-like branching pattern and its creeping growth habit along logs and rocks. The 'wort' part is an old English word meaning 'plant,' commonly used for small, humble plants that were once thought to have medicinal uses.
description: Creeping Fingerwort is a tiny liverwort that forms delicate, lacy mats on decaying wood and moist rocks. This miniature plant creates intricate branching patterns that look like tiny green fingers reaching across surfaces. It's so small that you'll need to look closely to appreciate its beautiful, fern-like structure. The entire plant rarely grows more than an inch or two across, making it one of our more subtle woodland residents.

idTips.label: Branching Pattern
idTips.description: Look for regularly divided, finger-like branches that split repeatedly in a feathery pattern, creating an almost fern-like appearance when viewed up close

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, creeping mats that hug tightly to surfaces, feeling almost papery to the touch and appearing translucent when backlit

idTips.label: Leaf Arrangement
idTips.description: Tiny leaves are arranged in three rows along the stem, with two side rows and one underneath, giving branches a slightly three-dimensional quality

idTips.label: Color and Texture
idTips.description: Fresh specimens are bright green to yellowish-green, becoming brownish when dry, with a delicate, almost tissue-paper texture

idTips.label: Size Scale
idTips.description: Individual branches are hair-thin and rarely exceed half an inch long, requiring close examination to see the intricate details

habitat: Look for Creeping Fingerwort on rotting logs, tree bases, and moist rock faces in shaded forests throughout New England. It thrives in humid environments where moisture lingers, often growing alongside other mosses and liverworts. You'll find it most commonly in mature deciduous and mixed forests with plenty of decaying wood.

seasonality.spring: Most visible and vibrant as moisture from snowmelt keeps it plump and bright green. This is the best time to spot its intricate branching patterns.
seasonality.summer: Remains visible in consistently moist spots but may appear smaller and less vibrant during dry periods. Look in the shadiest, dampest locations.
seasonality.fall: Often becomes more noticeable again as autumn rains return, taking on richer green colors against fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Persists under snow cover and can be found year-round, though it may appear brownish or dormant during the coldest months.

funFact: Despite being one of the smallest plants in New England forests, Creeping Fingerwort has conquered the entire planet—it's found on every continent except Antarctica, making this tiny forest dweller one of nature's most successful global travelers!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small leafy liverworts or delicate mosses. The key difference is Creeping Fingerwort's distinctly regular, finger-like branching pattern—other similar plants tend to have more irregular or simple branching. Remember: 'Fingers that creep' for the regular, hand-like branch divisions.
contextualKnowledge: Like all liverworts, Creeping Fingerwort represents an ancient lineage of plants that evolved before true mosses and ferns. The term 'liverwort' comes from medieval times when people thought these plants resembled liver lobes and could cure liver ailments—though of course, they have no medicinal properties.
compareHints: As the only Lepidozia species commonly found in New England, Creeping Fingerwort is most easily confused with other small leafy liverworts in different families. However, its consistently three-ranked leaf arrangement and regular branching pattern distinguish it from most relatives. Unlike many other liverworts that have more irregular growth, Creeping Fingerwort maintains its neat, geometric branching even as colonies spread.
